headline: Rates Hold Near Two-Week Low Despite Stock Rebound
tileReason: The daily 30-year average edged up just 0.01% to 7.34% Monday even as stocks staged their best day since April 2025, and the 10-year yield is slightly lower this morning.
takeaway:
Rates barely budged on Monday. Mortgage News Daily's 30-year average rose to 7.34% from 7.33% Friday, a change of just 0.01%, keeping rates near their lowest level since Nov 10. Other surveys taken Monday were lower: Zillow showed 7.14% and the Mortgage Research Center about 7.15%.

A huge stock rally failed to knock bonds off course. The S&P 500 jumped 4.7% Monday, its best day since April 2025, after Nvidia brought back Jensen Huang as CEO and its shares soared about 31%. When money rushes into stocks it often comes out of bonds, and Treasury yields did spike right after the 9 AM ET news, but they recovered most of that by the close. The 10-year Treasury yield, which mortgage rates tend to follow, ended Monday at about 4.92%, unchanged from Friday (some sources show it a few hundredths higher).

Falling oil helped cushion the blow. U.S. crude fell almost 4% Monday to about $80 a barrel, its lowest close since late August. Cheaper energy eases inflation worries, which makes bonds more attractive and helps hold rates down. Lenders started Monday with slightly higher rates, then trimmed them during the day as bonds steadied.

This morning the 10-year yield is a little lower, near 4.89%. Shortly after 7 AM PT, though, the Conference Board's consumer confidence index jumped to 103.3, far above the 92.5 forecasters expected and the highest since January 2025. A stronger-feeling consumer tends to push rates up, so watch whether that holds today. The government also sells $70 billion of 5-year notes at 10 AM PT; weak demand at these sales can nudge yields higher.

A December Fed hike now looks close to certain in the futures market. After New York Fed President John Williams said Monday that inflation, running near 3.5% on the Fed's preferred measure, is too high and that he wouldn't rule out raising rates at back-to-back meetings, futures markets (where traders bet on the Fed's next move) put the odds of a quarter-point increase on Dec 9 at about 96% to 98%, up from about 88% to 92% Friday. These are market expectations, not a Fed forecast.

Lenders still have a cushion. The Optimal Blue conforming index, which tracks rates on loans borrowers actually locked, sat about 2.19% above the 10-year Treasury on Nov 17, the latest day recorded, compared with a long-run average of about 1.76%. That extra room means lenders don't have to pass along every bit of a bond selloff.

Wednesday is the big test of this short week. At 5:30 AM PT we get October PCE inflation (the Fed's preferred measure of consumer prices), expected to rise 0.3% for the month, plus a second look at third-quarter growth. Bond markets close Thursday for Thanksgiving and close early Friday. After that: the Dec 4 jobs report, the Dec 9 Fed decision and November consumer prices on Dec 10.

drivers.title: Stock surge pulls money from bonds
drivers.text: Stocks had their best day since April 2025 Monday after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO. Money flowing into stocks usually comes partly out of bonds, and Treasury yields jumped right after the news, but bonds recovered most of that by the close, so mortgage rates rose only 0.01%.

drivers.title: Oil drops to a three-month low
drivers.text: U.S. crude fell almost 4% Monday to about $80 a barrel, its lowest close since late August. Cheaper energy eases inflation fears, which makes bonds more appealing and helped offset the stock rally's pull on yields.

drivers.title: Fed hike odds climb after Williams
drivers.text: New York Fed President John Williams said inflation is still too high and he wouldn't rule out hikes at back-to-back meetings. Futures odds of a Dec 9 hike rose to about 96%-98%. When investors expect the Fed to keep raising its short-term rate, longer-term yields and mortgage rates have a hard time falling far.

drivers.title: Consumers suddenly feeling better
drivers.text: Consumer confidence jumped to 103.3 this morning, far above the 92.5 expected and the highest since January 2025. Confident consumers spend more, which can keep inflation sticky, and that tends to push bond yields and mortgage rates up.

drivers.title: Mortgage rates still far above Treasuries
drivers.text: The Optimal Blue conforming index sat about 2.19% above the 10-year Treasury yield on Nov 17, compared with a long-run average of about 1.76%. That wide gap is a cushion: lenders can absorb part of a jump in Treasury yields, and have room to lower rates if bonds improve.

outlook.baseSource: Mortgage News Daily, Nov 23 close (latest available)
outlook.basis: The odds are close to even, tilted slightly higher. Rates held near a two-week low Monday even through a huge stock rally, which shows some underlying support from falling oil and a wide gap between mortgage rates and Treasuries (about 2.19% vs. a long-run average near 1.76%). Working against borrowers: a December Fed hike now looks nearly certain after Williams' remarks, consumer confidence just surged, and inflation reports keep running hot. Big swing events: the Nov 25 report on the Fed's preferred inflation measure, the Dec 4 jobs report, the Dec 9 Fed decision, Dec 10 consumer prices and oil headlines.
outlook.caveat: This is professional judgment from 30+ years watching these markets, not a guarantee. One oil headline or data surprise can move rates a quarter point in a day.

talkingPoints.buyers: Mortgage rates held near a two-week low Monday, with the daily 30-year average at 7.34%, even as stocks surged. But a December Fed hike now looks nearly certain and Wednesday's inflation report could move rates either way before the holiday. If you're under contract or close to it, talk with Stuart about how locking, a float-down option (which lets you take a lower rate if rates drop after you lock), or waiting would each fit your closing date.
talkingPoints.sellers: Rates are holding near 7.34%, a bit better than earlier this month, and buyers are feeling more confident according to this morning's survey. Realistic pricing, or a seller credit buyers can use to lower their rate, can help a home stand out heading into the holidays.
talkingPoints.oneLiner: Mortgage rates held steady near 7.34% Monday even as stocks had their best day in a year and a half, ahead of Wednesday's key inflation report.
